title: Four levers, one window
spec: M02B · add / compress / retrieve / offload on the same 9,685-token turn
intro: Take the six-layer inventory this module builds — 9,685 tokens, of which the user's question is 85 — and pull each lever on it in turn. Watch which layer each one moves, and which one loses.

provenance.source: the starting window is the module's own SIX_LAYERS inventory (system 420 · tools 1,180 · history 3,250 · retrieved 2,800 · tool results 1,950 · current turn 85). The per-lever figures are projections onto that window, not a measured run; step 5 carries the lab's measured table and cites it.

foot: The measured version — four arms over a real poisoned transcript — is labs/M02B-context-levers/

steps.title: The turn, itemised
narrative: One question, asked mid-session: who calls decode_jwt, and is the WAU definition in the docs the current one? Before the model reads a word of it, here is what else is in the window with it.

Six line items, 9,685 tokens. The message the user actually typed is 85 of them — 0.9%. When the answer comes back wrong, the reflex is to rewrite those 85 tokens. The other 99.1% is where the answer lives or dies.
So stop rewriting and start budgeting. Everything you can do about this window is one of four levers, and each one moves a different line.
steps.youDo: Before optimising anything, itemise. Print the token count of each of the six layers in your own agent's next turn — you cannot attack the biggest line until you know which one it is.

view.label: 200K window
view.note: The highlighted layer is the question. History and retrieved together are 6,050 tokens — 62% of the budget — and neither of them was asked for on this turn.

steps.title: add — the reflex, and its bill
narrative: The first instinct when an agent answers badly is to tell it more. Drop a 340-line root CLAUDE.md into the system layer — the architecture, the conventions, the metric definitions, the deploy runbook — and the agent will surely stop guessing.

It does stop guessing about a few things. It also now pays ~4,200 tokens on every session, including the ones that never touch billing or metrics, and the window grows from 9,685 to 13,885. The question you asked is now 0.6% of the context.

add is the only lever anyone can pull without infrastructure, which is exactly why it is the default failure mode. It is not wrong — M12's layered, directory-scoped CLAUDE.md is add done properly, carrying repo-wide facts and nothing else. Done improperly it is the everything-file, and inclusion is a cost, not a kindness.
steps.youDo: Count the lines in your repo's root CLAUDE.md. Then ask which of them the last five sessions actually needed.

view.label: 200K window
view.note: The system layer is 420 tokens: identity, a few standing rules.

view.label: 200K window
view.note: +43% on the window, paid on every turn of every session — including the ones that never touch a single fact in the file. This is the one lever that can make the budget worse, and it is the one everybody reaches for first.

steps.title: compress — same information, fewer tokens
narrative: Now aim at the layer that grew from exploration: tool results, 1,950 tokens of grep output and file dumps the agent accumulated working out where decode_jwt lives.

compress replaces that with a summary built once and reused by everyone — the ~700-token orientation read out of GRAPH_REPORT.md. Same territory covered, a third of the tokens, and the summary was generated at extraction time rather than re-derived by this session.
The window falls to 8,435. Note what compress does not do: it still describes exploration that happened. The next lever asks why the exploration happened at all.
steps.claudeSays: The agent reads one generated report section instead of the transcript of its own search. The compression cost was paid once, offline, by the build.

view.label: 200K window
view.note: Grep output, two whole-file reads, and the transcript of both.

view.label: 200K window
view.note: −1,250 tokens, −13% on the window. Built once by graphify update ., read by every session that follows — that reuse is what makes compress an infrastructure lever rather than a per-conversation trick.

steps.title: retrieve — don't summarise the search, replace it
narrative: Same layer, sharper attack. Instead of compressing the record of an exploration, ask a structural question and carry only its answer: explore("decode_jwt") returns kind, location, callers, callees and blast radius as one compact composite — about 180 tokens.

The window falls to 7,915, below the compressed arm, and something less obvious improves too. Five facts spread across five tool results sit in the middle of a long context, where recall is worst; one short composite adjacent to the question has no middle to get lost in.

This is the lever Track 2 exists to industrialise. The query is nearly free because the expensive part — parsing and indexing — already happened at extract time, and the answer is a stored structural fact rather than three leads you would have to verify by reading files.
steps.youDo: In your own stack, find the biggest tool-results turn of the week and ask: was that a question a pre-built index could have answered in one call?

view.label: 200K window
view.note: A shorter account of an exploration that still had to happen.

view.label: 200K window
view.note: 1,950 → 180 against the baseline. Note the trade the tools layer makes: 1,180 tokens of schemas are the price of admission for this lever, which is why M09 ships composite tools instead of a dozen narrow ones.

steps.title: offload — and which lever wins is a property of your window
narrative: Two layers are still untouched and together they are 6,050 tokens: retrieved holds similarity-ranked chunks about the WAU metric, including a stale one; history still contains the whole argument about which definition is right, long since settled.

offload puts settled knowledge where it belongs — one canonical OKF concept file, ~340 tokens, kept honest by M08's enrichment hook — and lets the resolved debate leave the transcript. Alone it takes the window to 6,985. Combined with retrieve: 5,215, or 54% of the baseline, with every fact still present.

Now the caveat that keeps this honest. On this module's lab fixture the profile was different — tool results were 2,341 of 3,131 tokens, 75% of the budget — so there retrieve was the big winner at 34% of raw and offload only reached 89%. On this window, history and retrieved dominate, so offload wins bigger. Which lever pays is a property of your layer profile, not a ranking you can memorise. Itemise first.
